sentences.text: Hello, This is six Minute English from BBC Learning English.

sentences.text: I'm Phil.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: And I'm Beth.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: Love it or hate it, there's no doubt fast food is popular.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: Are you a fast food fan, Beth?

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: Um,

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: not really, no.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: I think sometimes it can be quite convenient, obviously, because it's quick, but not really.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: Well, whatever you think about them fast food brands like KFC, Domino's and, of course the big one, McDonald's, are incredibly successful.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: In this programme, we'll discussing the global spread fast food from its beginnings in 1950s America.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: As usual, we'll be learning some useful new words and phrases.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: But first, I have a question for you, Beth. Roughly how many fast food restaurants are there in the UK?

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: Is it a), 4,000, b), 42,000, or c), 4 million?

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: I'm going to go for b), 42,000 okay,

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: well, later on we'll find out the answer.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: In the United States, cheap and easy food like hamburgers, French fries, and milkshakes have been popular since the 1950s.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: Listen as Adam Chandler, author of the book drive-through dreams, which traces the history of American fast food, tells BBC World Service program The Food Chain how it all got started.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: At the heart of the story of fast food is a very anyone can do this sense.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: A lot of the company founders didn't have a college degree, who didn't have a high school degree in a lot of instances, didn't come from money, were oftentimes just people who were ready to plug themselves into a system that would work for them.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: And it did.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: It made opportunity very, very easy in a time when that was a new part of the American experience.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: So it was the American dream in a very small way that became the American dream in a very big way.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: The rise of fast food reflected the rise of American economic power after the Second World War.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: When Adam says that this lies at the heart of the story, he means it's the most important part of the story

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: In the 1950s, when the famous brands we know today were just beginning anyone with can-do attitude could sell fast food.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: A can-do attitude describes someone who is confident and determined to fix problems and achieve results.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: Which exactly what happened successful restaurants like Kentucky Fried Chicken and McDonald's many, these fast food brands symbolised The American dream the idea that anyone in the United States can achieve success through hard work and determination.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: The success of KFC, McDonald’s and the rest wasn't limited to America.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: Nowadays, you can visit two McDonald's on opposite sides of the planet and eat exactly the same meal.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: But not every country opened its arms in welcome the tiny island of Iceland, for one.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: Andy Sophia Fontaine, who used to work in McDonald's, now edits The Iceland Review.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: Here she tells BBC World Service programme The Food Chain how McDonald's got a frosty reception when it started selling burgers in Iceland's capital, Reykjavik.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: There's been a long-standing burger culture in Iceland.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: They have their own take on a hamburger, wherein they'll use lettuce and raw cucumbers and a type of fry sauce that's called a shop burger and that's been around for ages.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: Yeah, so McDonald's, they struggled to try to maintain a market.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: The final nail in the coffin was the global financial crisis in two thousand eight, two thousand nine.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: Iceland already had a long standing tradition of eating burgers, a tradition that had existed for a long time.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: For example, the Schalpul Bulgari, or shop burger, was a take on, or variation of, the American hamburger.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: McDonald’s weren't as successful in Iceland as they'd been elsewhere.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: And the global financial crash of 2008 was the final nail in the coffin, an event which caused the failure of something that had already started to go wrong.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: To this day, there are no McDonald's in Iceland, unlike Britain, which reminds me of your question, Phil.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: Yes, I asked you how many fast food restaurants there are in Britain.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: I asked you if there were four thousand, forty two thousand or four million, And of course the answer is forty two thousand, so you were right well done.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: Okay, let's recap the vocabulary we've learned, starting with at the heart of, meaning the most important part or the cause of something.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: If you say that someone has a can-do attitude, you mean they are confident to take action, fix problems, and deal with new challenges.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: The American dream is the belief that everyone in the USA has the opportunity to be successful and happy if they work hard.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: The adjective long standing means having existed for a long time.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: A take on something means a variation or new way of presenting it.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: And finally, the idiom the final nail in the coffin refers to an event that causes the final end of something that had already started to fail.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: Once again, our six minutes are up but why not head over to the BBC Learning English website where you'll find a worksheet and quiz especially for this program.

sentences.speaker: Beth
sentences.text: See you there soon.

sentences.speaker: Phil
sentences.text: Goodbye.
